analysis.one_liner: Requires hedge fund and private equity advisers to register with the SEC and report for systemic-risk oversight.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Banking Committee: no hearing, no vote, and it drew zero cosponsors before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2008 financial crisis, large private investment pools like hedge funds and private equity funds operated outside SEC registration because of an old exemption. This bill would have repealed that exemption, requiring their advisers to register with the Securities and Exchange Commission, keep records, and file reports the SEC could share with federal agencies monitoring systemic risk. It also tightened rules on foreign advisers doing business in the U.S. and shielded the SEC's supervisory reports from public disclosure requests.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors in private funds and the broader public, who would gain an SEC-eye view of the hedge fund, private equity, and venture capital industries after those sectors helped transmit the 2008 crisis. Federal regulators would gain legal authority to collect data needed to spot risks building across the financial system.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'private adviser' exemption in the Investment Advisers Act so that advisers to hedge funds, private equity funds, and venture capital funds must register with the SEC, leaving only genuinely foreign advisers exempt [S2][S3].

Authorizes the SEC to require registered advisers to maintain records and submit reports necessary for federal supervision of systemic risk, and to share that information with other federal agencies [S2][S3].
Removes a old legal disclaimer that barred the SEC from requiring advisers to disclose client identities and investments, closing a gap in oversight [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private fund advisers — hedge fund, private equity, and venture capital managers — who would bear registration, recordkeeping, and reporting costs, some of which would likely be passed on to fund investors through fees. The bill also would let the SEC keep its confidential supervisory reports hidden from Freedom of Information Act requests.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hedge fund and private equity managers

drawbacks.text: Registration and reporting impose real compliance costs on private fund advisers, and smaller managers would feel them most; those costs can be passed to fund investors through fees [S3].
The bill shields SEC supervisory reports from public disclosure, so the added oversight would be visible to regulators but not to the public or press [S2][S3].
Registration itself does not restrict what hedge funds can do; it creates a watchdog paper trail but does not directly limit risky strategies or prevent future losses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is meaningful: bringing a large, lightly supervised corner of finance under SEC observation directly addresses the kind of blind spot that made the 2008 crisis worse. The costs are modest by comparison — registration and paperwork for fund managers, plus the tradeoff that the new oversight would be confidential rather than public. It is a transparency and information bill, not a restriction on fund activity, so its protection depends on regulators actually using the data.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it, so it died without a hearing or a vote; Congress enacted nearly identical hedge fund registration requirements in the Dodd-Frank law the following year.

narrative.text: Sen. Jack Reed introduced the bill on June 16, 2009 [S5][S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5].
No further action was taken — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The hedge fund and private equity industries, which avoided this standalone registration mandate — though Congress wrote substantially the same requirement into the Dodd-Frank financial law the following year, so the industry's escape was temporary.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hedge fund and private equity managers

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Christopher Dodd (D-CT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in June 2009 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — letting it die when the Congress ended

against.name: Hedge fund and private equity industry
against.role: Private fund managers facing new SEC registration
against.what_they_did: Opposed adviser registration requirements through lobbying during the 2009 financial regulation debate

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and the bill had zero cosponsors, so the record shows no party alignment either way.

industries.note: The bill repeals the exemption that let them operate without SEC registration, imposing registration, recordkeeping, and reporting duties. Their interest in staying outside SEC view ran against the public's interest in systemic risk oversight after the 2008 crisis.

industries.industry: Private equity and venture capital managers
industries.note: The bill's title expressly covers advisers to private equity and venture capital funds, ending their regulatory-free status and adding compliance costs.
The SEC gains registration jurisdiction over private fund advisers and authority to collect systemic-risk data, while getting confidentiality protection for its supervisory reports.
